text:
representing number is an actual credence. Several results named in
this chapter are reported but not proved here. Their primary sources,
as the chapter's reference list identifies them
\parencite[pp.~249--251]{HajekStaffel2021Dynamics}, form the following
finite set. Savage's representation theorem: L.~J. Savage,
\emph{The Foundations of Statistics} (New York: Wiley, 1954). Jeffrey's
alternative axioms and Bolker's representation theorem, which the
authors report as cited by Jeffrey and for which they give no separate
reference: R.~C. Jeffrey, \emph{The Logic of Decision} (Chicago:
University of Chicago Press, 1965). The Dutch-book theorem attributed to
Ramsey and de Finetti: F.~P. Ramsey, ``Truth and probability'' (1926
manuscript), in D.~H. Mellor (ed.), \emph{Philosophical Papers}
(Cambridge University Press, 1990), pp.~52--94; and B. de Finetti,
``Foresight: its logical laws, its subjective sources'' (French
original 1937), in H.~E. Kyburg and H.~E. Smokler (eds.),
\emph{Studies in Subjective Probability} (New York: Wiley, 1964),
pp.~100--110. Its converse: J.~G. Kemeny, ``Fair bets and inductive
probabilities'', \emph{Journal of Symbolic Logic} 20(3) (1955),
263--273. The general distance characterizations of conditioning and
Jeffrey conditioning: P. Diaconis and S. Zabell, ``Updating subjective
probability'', \emph{Journal of the American Statistical Association}
77(380) (1982), 822--830; the finite-partition cases are
\cref{thm:p15-rat41-minimal-update}. The results on approximate
coherence: G. De Bona and J. Staffel, ``Graded incoherence for
accuracy-firsters'', \emph{Philosophy of Science} 84(2) (2017),
189--213, and ``Why be (approximately) coherent?'', \emph{Analysis}
78(3) (2018), 405--415, with the earlier treatments the authors cite,
M.~J. Schervish, T. Seidenfeld and J.~B. Kadane, ``Measuring
incoherence'', \emph{Sankhy\=a} 64 (2002), 561--587, and L. Zynda,
``Coherence as an ideal of rationality'', \emph{Synthese} 109(2)
(1996), 175--216. No theorem proved in this chapter uses any of these
reported results as a premise.

\((0.3,0.4)\) as \(C^*(p)=0.438\), \(C^*({\sim}p)=0.572\)

objectives.

text:
For the reversed orientation, let \(q\) be a probability pair. If some
\(q_i=0\), the term \(c_i\log_2(c_i/q_i)\) is \(+\infty\) because
\(c_i>0\). Otherwise, since \(c=s_0\bar c\) and \(\sum_i\bar c_i=1\),
\[
 \sum_i c_i\log_2\frac{c_i}{q_i}
   =s_0\sum_i\bar c_i\Bigl(\log_2\frac{\bar c_i}{q_i}+\log_2s_0\Bigr)
   =s_0\bigl(D(\bar c,q)+\log_2s_0\bigr).
\]
As \(s_0>0\), Gibbs nonnegativity again makes \(q=\bar c\) the unique
minimizer. For every probability pair \(q\),
\(\sum_i(c_i-q_i)=s_0-1\) is constant, so adding it to the first
objective leaves its unique minimizer \(\bar c\) unchanged. Finally
\(\bar c=(0.42857\ldots,0.57142\ldots)\), which rounds to
\((0.429,0.571)\).
